original_question: If c > 1 is not an integer, is the sequence [n^c] good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations? More strongly, for every system (X, X, µ, T1, ..., Tℓ) and bounded functions f1, ..., fℓ, is the L2-limit of (1/N) Σ T1^[n^c] f1 · ... · Tℓ^[n^c] fℓ equal to the L2-limit of the linear averages (1/N) Σ T1^n f1 · ... · Tℓ^n fℓ?
target_in_paper: Section 6.2, Problem 29: the open problem asking whether the fractional-power integer-part sequence a(n)=⌊n^c⌋ is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations, together with the stronger claim that the corresponding L^2-averages should have the same limit as the linear averages. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right sequence, the right ambient setting (commuting transformations), the two properties the paper asks about (multiple recurrence and multiple convergence), and the paper’s stronger limit-formula clause comparing the ⌊n^c⌋-averages with the linear averages. That is very close to the official target. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
missing_details: The official problem is phrased for noninteger c, not only for c>1; your draft narrows the scope to the harder subrange c>1, but that is slightly narrower than the paper’s stated formulation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

To be fully stand-alone, the system should be written as a probability space (X, 𝓧, μ) with commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T_1, ..., T_ℓ:X→X, and the test functions should be specified as f_1, ..., f_ℓ ∈ L^∞(μ). ([math.uoc.gr](https://www.math.uoc.gr/~nikosf/OpenProblems/OpenProblems.pdf?utm_source=openai))
The quantifier 'for every ℓ∈N' should be made explicit; in the paper, 'multiple' means that the corresponding ℓ-fold property holds for every ℓ. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

The recurrence part should be unpacked explicitly: for every A∈𝓧 with μ(A)>0, there should exist n∈N such that μ(A ∩ T_1^{-⌊n^c⌋}A ∩ ··· ∩ T_ℓ^{-⌊n^c⌋}A) > 0. This is the paper’s formal meaning of 'good for multiple recurrence of commuting transformations' for a single sequence. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
The convergence part should be stated as L^2(μ)-convergence of the averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^{⌊n^c⌋}f_1 ··· T_ℓ^{⌊n^c⌋}f_ℓ. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
The stronger clause should specify that the comparison is with the L^2-limit of the linear averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^n f_1 ··· T_ℓ^n f_ℓ. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
It is better to replace the paper’s bracket notation [n^c] by the unambiguous floor notation ⌊n^c⌋. ([math.uoc.gr](https://www.math.uoc.gr/~nikosf/OpenProblems/OpenProblems.pdf?utm_source=openai))
refined_question: Let c>0 be a noninteger real number and set a(n)=⌊n^c⌋. Is it true that a(n) is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations, in the following precise sense: for every ℓ∈N, every probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), every commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T_1, ..., T_ℓ:X→X, and every A∈𝓧 with μ(A)>0, does there exist n∈N such that μ(A ∩ T_1^{-a(n)}A ∩ ··· ∩ T_ℓ^{-a(n)}A)>0; and, for every f_1, ..., f_ℓ∈L^∞(μ), do the averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^{a(n)}f_1 ··· T_ℓ^{a(n)}f_ℓ converge in L^2(μ)? More strongly, is this L^2-limit always equal to the L^2-limit of the linear averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^n f_1 ··· T_ℓ^n f_ℓ? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
justification: This draft clearly targets Section 6.2, Problem 29, rather than any neighboring problem: the paper there asks about the sequence [n^c] for commuting transformations and then adds the stronger claim that the associated L^2-limit should coincide with the limit of the linear averages. To make the question self-contained and faithful to the paper, I unpacked the defined phrases 'good for multiple recurrence of commuting transformations' and 'good for multiple convergence of commuting transformations' using the definitions from Sections 3.1 and 3.2. I did not broaden the problem beyond the paper’s intent; I only made explicit the hidden quantifiers and hypotheses that the paper leaves packaged inside its terminology. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
